speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ALLEGED DIFFICULTY IN OBTAINING APPLICATION FORMS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Is the minister aware that some persons in British Columbia are complaining that they cannot yet obtain the application forms for disabled persons' pensions from the offices of the government of British Columbia? Has the minister received any word from the government of British Columbia as to when application forms will be issued, and is the situation in British Columbia in this regard different from that prevailing in the rest of the country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ALLEGED DIFFICULTY IN OBTAINING APPLICATION FORMS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member gave me notice of his intention to ask pretty much the question which he has now put. On November 13 a draft agreement under the Disabled Persons Act was sent to the province of British Columbia and the agreement has not yet been returned. As soon as it is we will give the matter our immediate attention and the province will be in a position, in accordance with its own law, to carry out the act in such a manner as to provide pensions under this act for the citizens of British Columbia.

subtopic: ALLEGED DIFFICULTY IN OBTAINING APPLICATION FORMS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: How many provinces thus far have returned the draft agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ALLEGED DIFFICULTY IN OBTAINING APPLICATION FORMS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
As of this date only one agreement has been completed, that with the province of New Brunswick. The provinces of Saskatchewan. Nova Scotia and Alberta have signed agreements. These are now being processed at this end, and in a very few days they should be completed. In the case of Prince Edward Island an interim form of agreement has been signed and returned by the provincial minister. The government of Prince Edward Island proposes to pass legislation at the forthcoming session of the legislature to make this agreement effective. In the meantime we have asked for its proposed scheme of administration, which is necessary under the act.
In the case of the provinces of Newfoundland, Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia draft agreements were sent on November 18, as I indicated a moment ago in the case of British Columbia. The replies have not all reached us yet. In the case of the province of Quebec a draft agreement was sent to the provincial government on November 18. We are now awaiting the return of the signed agreement from this province.

subtopic: CESSATION OF LAY-OFFS AND REINSTATEMENT OF THOSE ALREADY LAID OFF

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: CESSATION OF LAY-OFFS AND REINSTATEMENT OF THOSE ALREADY LAID OFF
speechtext: On Monday last the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked whether I could give the assurance that we are at the end of lay-offs by the Canadian National Railways, and if I could say how soon those laid off in recent months would be reinstated. I should like to reply to the hon. member. The management of the railway informs me that reductions in working forces have been a necessary consequence of the general decline in traffic and that the volume of traffic determines in a very large measure how many persons the railway can employ. Because a general increase in traffic depends on such economic factors as industrial production and trade, it is not possible to say when an improvement in traffic conditions will justify the reinstatement of those whom it has been necessary to lay off.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, January 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Yves Leduc (Verdun) for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Rowe, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
May I first join in congratulating the mover (Mr. Leduc) and seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address. They are both young men of great promise who acquitted themselves well and made a great impression in the house. In time they will, I believe, leave their mark on Canadian public life.
The speech from the throne has in it one paragraph of particular interest to the Canadian people, which should be discussed at some length. I have reference to the following, and I quote:
The National Housing Act. 1954, enacted early in the last session, which authorized lower downpayments and larger loans, and which enabled the chartered banks for the first time to make loans on the security of residential mortgages, has been an important factor in stimulating the construction of a record number of houses in the past year. The prospects are favourable for a high level of house building in 1955.
Originally I had intended to speak of the great achievement of the department, but the full statistics are not yet available. If other members do not exhaust this subject during the course of the debate I intend later to

latch on to the omnibus amendment and review the accomplishments indicated in that particular part of the address.
There is another part of the address which is of immediate concern and will be of benefit to the Canadian people. It reads as follows:
It is proposed to bring into general operation on the first of February the provision of the act under which loans may be made for home improvements. In accordance with an undertaking given at the last session, this section was proclaimed for small holders under the Veterans' Land Act with effect from the first of this year.
The proclamation of the home improvement section of the housing act on the first of February is indeed a commendable step, and particularly welcome at this time when it is more likely to be fruitful by reason of the participation of the banks in making funds available. This section could lead to opportunities for the improvement and modernization of homes all across Canada. I take this first opportunity to emphasize that the Canadian people are initially and vitally concerned with the number of new homes erected rather than with those that have new bathtubs or new garages, important as they certainly are. The emphasis must remain on new homes. We cannot afford to be diverted from our ultimate objective to continue to set housing records year after year. I just indicate to the house that loans under the home improvement section will carry a government insurance guarantee to the banks and other approved lenders, and the borrower will pay a 1 per cent premium.
Today I intend to direct my remarks to what I consider to be an inequality which now exists under the act and which, in my view, should be corrected at a very early date. Those who are intimately acquainted with the National Housing Act will know that it was based on one primary assumption, that it is in the public interest for as many Canadians as possible in the middle and lower income groups to own their own homes. The act is not very much concerned with people who can go out and buy their homes in the open market, make a large down payment and arrange their own financing privately. It is primarily designed to help the 52 per cent of Canadians who, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, earn less than $3,000 a year.
The National Housing Act has encouraged the building and owning of lower cost homes by the following method: Lower interest rates and subsidization; lower down payments and longer amortization periods; standardization of design in order to reduce costs; making mortgage money easily available. As a direct result of the housing legislation passed at the last session of parliament mortgage money
The Address-Mr. Croll has become available at every whistle stop in Canada wherever the banks have outlets, and there are more than 4,000 of them. Indeed, this particular act has made it possible for more Canadians than ever to own their own homes. It has succeeded where private industry has failed. I think it is important that we do not let the act rest on its laurels. It must be continually revised and improved in the light of changing conditions.
One revision which I believe should be seriously considered now is a means whereby the home owner's basic equity, and by that I mean nis down payment, can be protected against personal reverses. Let me elaborate for a moment. Let us consider the position of the average prospective home owner under the National Housing Act. He is a worker who, on the national average, is earning about $3,000 a year. Depending upon where he is living, he may be earning slightly more or slightly less than that amount. In my own province of Ontario he is earning $62.58 a week or just over $3,300, which is just above the minimum requirements under the present act.
In order to buy a home under the National Housing Act this average Canadian must make a down payment of at least $1,500, or one-half of his annual income. I am using the $10,000 home as an example, but there are homes being built in Ontario under the National Housing Act for less than $10,000- and they are being sold for less than that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mostly more than that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: In most cases the cost is more than that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If the owner has been lucky he may have been able to save the amount of the down payment out of his earnings. Chances are that he may have to go out and borrow some of the money from his friends in order to make the down payment. In many instances that down payment represents the family savings. In any case it is probably all the money he has in the world, and he is investing in the biggest and most important purchase in all his life.
Let us not underestimate the seriousness of the step that man is taking. We can be sure that he is carefully considering all the probabilities. He will consider that he is investing his life savings in a new home, and he will realize that, later, if some unexpected contingency should arise he will have no reserves with which to meet the occasion. That is something that makes him stop and think. He will consider whether his present and his potential earnings are adequate to carry the mortgage of $8,500 or more, together with
110	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Croll taxes, heating, and all the upkeep of a home, including furnishings. He will give consideration to what might happen if he should become sick or unemployed, or if he should die before the mortgage obligation is fully discharged. Naturally he will want desperatelv to be able to pay off his home, and he expects that he will do so. But at the same time he must consider what is going to happen if he fails to keep up his payments. If he is over 40 he will remember the foreclosures and the tax sales of the thirties, and he will wonder whether it cannot happen again.
These are surely some of the thoughts that will run through his mind as he prepares to invest his hard-earned $1,500 or more in a home. He hopes he will be able to protect his investment. He hopes he will be able to make his payments, and he wonders what will happen if he cannot.
I believe it is the duty of the government, which is encouraging him to invest his all in a national housing home, to offer him a measure of protection. At the present time the government is protecting lending institutions by insuring the amount of the mortgage. With that I am in full accord and agreement. You can believe me that the lending institution, with its funds spread over thousands of investments, and secured in each case by property, is far less in need of protection than the national housing owner, who has all his eggs in one basket.
At the present time, and quite properly, the government protects the national housing mortgagee, and it is my view that it should protect the national housing owner, at least to the extent of his initial down payment. Every owner is far more vulnerable than the lending institution. No matter what happens the lending institution cannot lose. In the event of a foreclosure it will look first to the property, and then to the government for repayment. But the owner may very well be wiped out.
That is the situation that needs a remedy. Under the act the owner should be assured that if he is unable to keep up his payments, his basic equity of $1,500 or more, which is his down payment, will be protected under all circumstances, including the mortgage covenant, subject to certain limitations.
So far as the mechanics are concerned, it is no more difficult to strike a premium rate for the down payment, which I call equity insurance, than it was to strike a premium rate for the mortgage insurance. We had no previous experience when we fixed the 2 per cent premium rate on the mortgage. I am sure the same actuaries who fixed the rate on the guaranteed mortgages could fix the


rate on equity insurance. It should be 2 per cent, the same rate that applies to the mortgage.
I informed the house earlier that the rate was 1 per cent on home improvement loans made without mortgage security. If we used the 2 per cent figure-and it could be somewhat higher, or possibly lower-it would mean that for a premium of $30 on a down payment of $1,500 or $40 on a down payment of $2,000 the owner's equity would be fully insured. Then, in the event of default under the mortgage resulting in a foreclosure, the owner would have his basic equity returned -instead of being frozen out, as would most likely happen in the case of a foreclosure.
Obviously there would have to be safeguards against fraud and bad faith. The purpose of basic equity insurance would be to protect the owner, if he found it impossible to carry on. It would not be intended to let him skin out of a deal the next day simply because he changed his mind.
Government departments have had considerable experience in the insurance field, and I would expect regulations imposing conditions having regard to the element of time, the possibility of the death of the owner, of transferability, as well as a limit of the liability in the early stages. But if an owner meets these conditions and cannot keep up his payments, and foreclosure follows, he would be entitled then to the return of his basic equity, which was his original down payment, for which he has already paid an insurance premium. I strongly urge the government to introduce an amendment to cover such a situation.
It will first and foremost give security to the person who needs it most, namely, the home owner, who has a small equity and a good sized mortgage.

speechtext: Does the hon. member recall the answer the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) gave to the question I asked along that line last year? He said that he would give sympathetic consideration, but sympathy will not pay the owner.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am hoping for better luck than the hon. member had.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I hope you get it. You are on the other side of the house; you may get it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Don't try to get into this act; make your own speech.
As I have said, it seems highly incongruous to protect the lending institutions and not protect the owner. Both are making an investment in the same property at the same

time. If one is insured the other should be insured also. Under the act the owner pays a premium for the mortgage insurance. I see no reason why we should not extend the same protection to the home owner that we are prepared to give, and actually do give as a matter of course, to the lending institution. Both make an investment. One is protected fully, the other is not. I think it is no more than justice that the protection that we give to our lending institutions should be extended in a limited and a substantial form to the Canadians who make purchases under the National Housing Act.
It will not cost the Canadian taxpayers a penny, but it would encourage home ownership and possibly bring about larger down payments. It would remove the hazard to which too many of our people have been vulnerable in the past. I am convinced that such a plan would greatly stimulate national house building and home ownership, and avoid future bitterness.
Mortgage insurance removed the very last reluctance of the lending institutions to advance money on national housing mortgages. Equity insurance would have the same effect on the prospective owner. If both the lending institutions and the owner are to be insured against loss within the limits I have suggested, or within other reasonable limits, then I anticipate an immediate upswing in construction, with attendant benefits throughout our economy, with particular emphasis on employment, and, what is equally important, home ownership.
Equity insurance would put the little home owner on the same footing as the lending institutions, and it would give him protection and security at a price he can afford to pay. It would keep the little man from being seriously hurt in any economic squeeze play. He would know that no matter what happened to him the original stake would be secure. This an economic hurricane could not wash away. He asks the right to share the economic umbrella which he is now providing for the lending institutions.
Let there be no misunderstanding about one thing. I am not suggesting that the government should give anybody a handout. What I am proposing is a proper insurance scheme based on sound actuarial principles, as sound as those applied when they fixed the premium rate of 2 per cent on the mortgage. I am expecting that the owner will pay for his own protection.
By paying a premium into a government fund he could provide that protection, as he does now for the lending institutions, without benefit of government subsidy. His down
The Address-Mr. Croll payment on his home could never be lost through foreclosure. Nor am I anticipating for one moment that we are going to see a spate of foreclosures in the future. I sincerely believe that our economy is basically sound enough to weather whatever may be ahead. But in the lifetime of most of us in this house we have seen thousands of our citizens lose everything they have put into a house. The great depression of the 1930's forced us to realize that ownership of a home had in it an element of gamble; that a man and his family could find themselves on the street without a cent to show for years of saving.
It may be that what I propose and call equity insurance will remain a protection against a danger that may never occur. That is the way we would all want it to be. But we do not know. The storekeeper who protects his plate glass window by insurance does not expect it to be broken. Should it happen, it becomes little more than a temporary inconvenience. I feel it is a wise and prudent thing to insure against the possibility of loss. We would be more than foolish to bury our heads in the sand and leave the future to chance, when we do not need to do so. That is one of the reasons we established an unemployment insurance fund back in 1941. We were not expecting unemployment within the forseeable future. We did feel that in any economy there is always the possibility of some unemployment, and we set out to insure against that.
I want this house to believe that I am not attempting to sell the government a bill of goods. You know, I have not been very good at that. Nor am I enticing them down a blind alley. That would not be wise or politically profitable. I am suggesting that in line with the undertakings in the public interest, which the government has so well assumed and carried out in the past in the field of insurance, they might very well apply their experience and knowledge to this problem.
It would be profitable if I enumerated some of the insurance undertakings of this government. I have already spoken of unemployment insurance. It has been very successful. We have export credit insurance. Some members may know about that. They are doing a land office business. Their purpose is:
The corporation may, for the purpose of facilitating and developing trade between Canada and any other country, enter into a contract of insurance with an exporter to insure him against any risk of loss in connection with the export or an agreement for the export of goods by reason of the failure of the exporter, for any cause not avoidable by the exporter, to recover the selling price of the goods.

The Address-Mr. CroU
Hon. members will recall that at the last session we increased the capitalization of the export credit insurance corporation from $5 million to $15 million. We have the Prairie Farm Assistance Act which, though limited in scope, is insurance against the hazard of drought. Last session we passed the National Housing Act, which provided insurance for mortgages and rental insurance. I am sure the house will be interested to know that the banks have loaned nearly $115 million in less than six months. We have had proclaimed the home improvement section, which also has in it an element of insurance. I am sure no hon. member has forgotten the Public Service Insurance Act with which we grappled last session and which provided for certain death benefits. This act affects thousands of civil servants.
Hon. members may be less aware that we are also in the marine insurance business. The very able and energetic minister did not let grass grow under his feet when he took over the ministry of fisheries. As early as July, 1953, provision was made for the insuring of fishing vessels valued at from $250 to $7,500. A total of 1,200 policies were purchased in Newfoundland, 250 in Quebec and 351 in British Columbia, covering 2,300 boats with a value of over $3,500,000. This is the result of the last eighteen months' operation and it is expected that this total will increase to $10,000,000. The insurance provides full coverage, but what is more interesting is that this insurance provided by the Department of Fisheries costs only 1-6 per cent as against the commercial rate of 5 per cent and up.
I say that in praise of the minister but also to indicate to the house that we are not novices in this sort of thing that I am talking about.	|
All I am proposing is that we deal in the very same way with the problem of equity insurance because it is inevitable that some home owners will fall by the wayside in the foreseeable future and the only sensible thing to do is to spread the loss across the board by an insurance scheme. In that way no one will be hurt by circumstances beyond his control, and home ownership will be encouraged. Mortgage insurance is now compulsory under the act. Equity insurance would have to be compulsory also, since it could not work otherwise.
I do not make this proposal lightly. I realize that there are a great number of administrative difficulties. It may be the course of wisdom at the beginning not to insure the full down payment. In some circumstances that could be interpreted as insuring the
[Mr. Croll.l

owner against his own folly. Serious consideration would have to be given to a time lapse to avoid fraud and bad faith.
There will be other questions that will arise in your minds, but I suggest that it is administratively possible to draw up regulations to meet all conditions. This government has wrestled with far more difficult problems and has solved them to the lasting benefit of the Canadian people. I ask that the government give consideration to this problem and accept in principle what I have suggested. We can wait for improvements and refinements at a later date.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne in my opinion has one great value. It has many others, but it has at least the value that it enables members from different parts of our nation to explain to their fellow members the problems that are worrying the people of their constituencies. This is particularly important for those of us who come from British Columbia because that province is farther away from the centre of Canada than any other. Its resources and economy are different from those of the other provinces.
During the time that we are at home we find it difficult to follow closely what is taking place in the rest of Canada and I believe that the rest of Canada gets a great deal less news about British Columbia than we on the west coast get about what is happening east of the Rocky mountains. I have been pleased to note that already three hon. members from our province have participated in this debate and I hope that all the other members will express their views on the problems that are worrying our people at the present time.
I propose today to place before the cabinet and the house six different problems which in my opinion are of concern to the people on the west coast. The first is the question of unemployment.
We regret, as I am sure hon. members from other parts of Canada also regret, that unemployment has again become a serious problem in this nation. I think the speech from the throne dealt with it rather lightly. The only reference is contained in this one sentence:
Some unemployment of a regional and seasonal nature is being experienced.
I have no idea of the position with regard to unemployment in other parts of Canada, but certainly in British Columbia it is such that it merits far more serious consideration

than is implied by that sentence. In Vancouver private agencies such as the Salvation Army and others, and the various churches, have found the situation such that they have felt it necessary to step in and provide relief for the destitute. That has not been done to any extent in my city for quite a few years.
The city of Vancouver itself is also much concerned. The city council have been worrying about this problem and decided about three weeks ago that they would institute relief payments. The mayor summed up the attitude of the council very well, and I quote:
At the same time, Mayor Hume called for action on a national policy to handle the unemployment problem.
"I hope the Prime Minister and the premier will wake up", he declared.
He was referring to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) and the premier of the province. He went on to say:
There are a lot of people who can't find jobs- personally I don't know of one job In the city today.
About the same time our provincial premier wired the Prime Minister about this problem and made this recommendation:
After due consideration of all factors this government urges strongly that, with respect to unemployed employables, adequate relief be extended, and that the cost thereof be shared to the extent of 40 per cent by the government of Canada, 40 per cent by the government of this province and 20 per cent by the municipalities. Immediate attention to this problem is urged by this government.
To my amazement that suggestion received rather brusque treatment by the Prime Minister of Canada. Two days later the following press report appeared:
In a statement in Ottawa, Prime Minister St. Laurent said he had no evidence that B.C. was unable to bear the financial responsibility of prodding relief for those unemployed who are able to work.
In other words, if the province can pay the relief, then it must do so. The dominion will accept no responsibility. That, Mr. Speaker, is an evasion of responsibility by this government. Furthermore, it is a complete about-face from the stand taken by this very government in the year 1945, when it Drought down what are known as the "green 3ook" proposals.
I turn to these proposals and find this on page 42:
Over the past seven or eight years there have leen recommendations by the national employment lommission, the Sirois commission and others, that he dominion should assume responsibility for lecessary relief to the employable unemployed.
The Address-Mr. Green
That, I would point out, is the group about which Premier Bennett wired:
It has been generally suggested that the dominion should accept this obligation as part of any general settlement with the provinces.
The dominion has come to a settlement with all the provinces with the exception of Quebec, and apparently there is about to be some settlement with that province.
The "green book" proposals went on:
As a part of the general arrangement with the provincial governments, the dominion government now proposes to establish a practicable and comprehensive system of assistance to able-bodied unemployed persons as soon as possible, rather than waiting until the need for it actually arises.
This, remember, was in 1945:
It is thought necessary not to permit the recurrence of the problems of administration being separated from financial responsibility, and to avoid the makeshift arrangements and controversy with provincial governments which otherwise would be almost certain to recur under the old methods of providing relief even though the number of persons involved were small.
I would point out that we are now having this very controversy which the dominion suggested in 1945 should be avoided. The proposals go on:
The dominion is therefore accompanying its proposal for general acceptance of responsibility with a concrete plan for its implementation in the field of assistance for employable unemployed persons.
One further paragraph of significance to be found on page 43 reads as follows:
The plan proposes acceptance of dominion responsibility for unemployed employables, and provincial and local responsibility for unemplov-ables.
This government is today repudiating the stand it took in 1945. This federal government has an obligation with regard to the employable unemployed. In the case of British Columbia most of them come from outside the province. As a result of the refusal of the Prime Minister to accept any responsibility, the premier of British Columbia has stated, "All right, we will pay 80 per cent of the relief. The city can pay the other 20 per cent, but it will be paid only to those recipients who have established residence of one year in the province of British Columbia". All the rest are thrown on the charitable organizations. I suggest the time has come for this government to accept its responsibility in this regard. This trouble will probably arise every year, and this is only the start of it. Sooner or later the problem will have to be faced by the dominion government. Now is the time to take action.
The second question has to do with Columbia river power. There is a reference to that

The Address-Mr. Green in the speech from the throne, although it does not mention the Columbia river. I refer to the paragraph which reads as follows:
Amendments to the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act and a measure to control works which affect the normal flow of rivers which cross the international boundary will be proposed for the purpose of ensuring that .natural resources are developed in the best interests of the Canadian public.
The very last line of that paragraph seems to indicate that the government has now adopted a Canada-first policy. If that were the whole story I would approve, and I am very glad that at last the government seems to be moving in the direction of adopting our Canada-first policy.
Hon. members will recall how in recent years we have had to hammer this government night in and night out, during private members' hour, to prevent it from supporting a proposal to build a natural gas pipe line from southern Alberta down into the United States at the nearest point to serve the great cities of Washington and Oregon, with only a stub line up to Vancouver and possibly one to Trail. As a result of a filibuster staged largely by this party, with the help of the C.C.F., and the former Liberal member for Fraser Valley, George Cruickshank, the government was eventually convinced that a Canada-first policy was advisable. Just a few weeks ago we had an announcement that natural gas is to be piped from the Peace river country down through the centre of the province of British Columbia to serve practically all the cities in that province, with the surplus going into the United States. We also had some trouble with regard to a natural gas pipe line from Alberta to eastern Canada, and it took quite a lot of pressure and argument to convince the government this should be an all-Canadian line. However, it finally adopted that policy.
In so far as the plans of the government with regard to the Columbia river system are concerned, we approve of anything which means the use of Canadian resources by the Canadian people. But I am afraid the story is not quite that simple. I believe this proposal is also designed as a club with which to beat the government of the province of British Columbia. That government, rightly or wrongly, has come to an agreement with the Kaiser interests in the United States under which there is to be a dam constructed across the foot of the Arrow lakes so that water will be stored in the Arrow lakes as a result of which more power will be available for United States plants south of the line.
The dominion government has taken objection to this plan, and we now have the picture

of the two governments through their respective ministers calling each other names. For example, I have here the Vancouver Sun for November 25, 1954, carrying the headline: "Ottawa Dam Stand called 'Cheap Trick'." That is a statement by Premier Bennett. Then we have a statement by his minister of lands on November 30. The report of his speech carries the heading: "Opponents of Dam 'Lack Information'." It adds: "Lands Minister Charges Ottawa Veto would be 'Denial of Rights' of B.C."
Then we have Ottawa moving into the picture. I have here a dispatch dated November 22, 1954, from Warren Baldwin, who we all know is one of the most responsible newspapermen in Canada. The heading reads, "Ottawa Moves to Block B.C.-Kaiser Power Deal" with the subheading "New Statute Being Drafted to Provide Authority."
Finally we have the old master, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), turning all his guns on the government of British Columbia in a statement dated December 30, 1954. It reads: "B.C.'s Kaiser Dam Project 'Cockeyed' says Howe." This is another dispatch from Ottawa by Mr. Baldwin:
Trade Minister C. D. Howe Wednesday described the agreement between the B.C. government and the Kaiser interests in the United States for a storage dam without on-site power on the Arrow lakes as "a cockeyed and improvident deal."
A war in print has been waged in the press between the two governments. The premier of British Columbia is sitting there ready to go to the courts about this issue and Ottawa is prepared to beat him into submission. I point out, Mr. Speaker, that power on the Columbia river system in Canada can only be developed by co-operation between the two governments. The main source of power is to be a dam at Mica creek up above Revelstoke on the Big Bend. That is certainly in British Columbia and the provincial government will certainly be the authority to deal with that dam.
The same British Columbia government has dealt with the huge project at Kitimat. That was not the business of the federal government at all. There must be co-operation between the two governments. I believe that both sides are sincere. The premier of British Columbia believes that he is making a deal which is for the benefit of his province and is doing no harm to the rest of Canada. The ministers here believe that the deal is not a good one and that it should be stopped. Let us admit that there is sincerity on both sides. All I wish to emphasize is that this fighting attitude is helping no one and is only going to make it more difficult to have the Columbia river system properly developed in so far as power is concerned.

Our main responsibility in this House of Commons is to see where parliament fits into the picture. So far we have only had newspaper reports. We have had shots from both sides. With the exception of the St. Lawrence, the Columbia river is the most important river in this country so far as power is concerned. In fact I believe that the two river systems have about the same potential. This is an extremely important problem for the Canadian people and for their parliament. It involves not only the Arrow lakes in West Kootenay but also the Kootenay river in East Kootenay and the Mica creek dam. It involves the whole question of downstream benefits and what is to be paid by the United States interests for storage of water on the system in Canada.
It may also involve the Fraser river. The suggestion has been made by federal ministers that they are going to divert some of the Columbia river water into the Fraser river. That may be a good idea but I point out that just six years ago we had terrible floods on the Fraser, and the people living in the delta of that river are very much concerned about what is going to happen to them if a lot of Columbia river water is diverted into the Fraser.
I suggest that the way for parliament to handle the question is to have it considered by the external affairs committee. In each of the last two sessions that committee has heard evidence on the Columbia river system from General McNaughton, and very interesting and useful evidence it was. If that committee is allowed to deal with the question this year before the proposed legislation becomes law, then General McNaughton can be called to explain the whole story. We can have representatives from the British Columbia government attend. We can crossexamine officials from the different federal government departments who have been studying the Columbia river system, and we might even have representatives from the Kaiser interests who could tell their side of the story.
My point is that this is the kind of problem that should be carefully studied by the private members of the house. It should not be left to one or two ministers to make a decision which will affect Canadians on the west coast for generations to come. If the government does not wish to refer the matter to the standing committee on external affairs, a special committee could be set up or a new committee could be set up to deal with all questions of power.
I was very much interested in an article in the Financial Post of October 23 last by Michael Barkway, another distinguished member of the press gallery, in which he
The Address-Mr. Green advocated a national energy policy for Canada. He advocated that all questions concerning power, whether it be power generated from water, atomic energy or in any other way, be dealt with together. I think his plan was excellent. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) promised that during this session there would be a committee on atomic energy. It might be possible to have a committee of that kind also consider the Columbia river situation.
My third subject has to do with the price of wheat in store at Vancouver. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce announced yesterday, the government adopted a new policy on February 16 of last year under which the Canadian wheat board varied the price of wheat as between Vancouver and Fort William-Port Arthur with the objective of making these centres competitive. That was a departure from the policy that had been followed from 1943, a policy under which prices were the same at the west coast and the lakehead. When changing the policy the minister dropped the price of wheat at Fort William-Port Arthur by 7 cents. One result of this change in policy has been that shipments of wheat out of Vancouver dropped 40 per cent during the last four months of last year compared with the same four months in 1953.
Vigorous protests have been made by a joint committee of the international longshoremen's and warehousemen's union and the grain workers' union in Vancouver. Incidentally, they have given splendid leadership on this matter. They have been supported by groups all over the city, by the city council, by the provincial government and by all of the papers. For example, I have here an editorial from the Vancouver Sun, which is a supporter of the government. The heading is, "Facts for Mr. Howe, All Port Interests Suffer as Grain Trade Declines". The editorial, published on December 22 last, reads:
There is a simple way for trade minister Howe to convince himself that the wheat board grain price juggling in favour of eastern ports is truly damaging Vancouver and citizens' wage packets. From Vancouver merchants exchange, national harbours board, shipping federation, stevedoring firms and waterfront unions, and ship supply, chandlery and repair firms, he will learn that fewer vessels are coming here to take grain. When year end figures are officially prepared they will show a decrease between July 31-end of the crop year-and December, 1954, compared with the same period 1953.
The Vancouver Province of January 7, five days ago, had an editorial headed "An Urgent Job for Vancouver M.P.'s" which reads in part as follows:
Vancouver members of parliament have a job to do at the session opening this week. They should

The Address-Mr. Green
make it their business to speak and work to end the federal discrimination against wheat shipments through this port.
The Vancouver Herald of January 3 this year had an editorial headed, "Let Mr. Howe now heed his own advice 'to keep all ports competitive'
The fact is that the wheat board in changing prices has always been one step behind. Ocean freight rates go up but the price does not drop as fast as these rates go up. The result has been that shipments of wheat through the port have fallen. Even with the removal of this difference in price, Vancouver would have great difficulty in meeting the Atlantic price, I believe. For one reason, it is a far longer voyage; it takes far longer for the wheat to get to the United Kingdom from the west coast. Shipping is not as plentiful as it is on the east coast. We believe that this policy, which the minister announced yesterday is to be permanent, is a wrong policy. It sets off Vancouver against the lakehead. Buyers take advantage of that fact. They wonder why there are two prices. When the price is dropped at Vancouver they wait to see if the price will not drop at Fort William.
This new control imposed by this free enterprise Minister of Trade and Commerce is unwise. I even took from his statement yesterday that he believes the west coast should sell its wheat in Japan and South America, around the Pacific, and not worry about the United Kingdom market. We are just as much concerned about the United Kingdom market as are the centres in other parts of Canada. I believe that in the long run the old policy would be far better, both for Vancouver and for Fort William-Port Arthur. We on the west coast demand that this discrimination be ended without further delay.
This question brings up my fourth point. The drop in shipping coming into Vancouver harbour for grain has meant fewer ships in that port to carry other commodities. We are now in the position where it is a great problem to get ships to carry our pulp. People who must ship these products abroad are finding it increasingly difficult to get bottoms. Canada has no deep sea dry cargo fleet. On the west coast there is not one ship left under Canadian registry. We are dependent on foreign ships to carry our goods. Here we are, the nation which per capita has to ship more of its goods than any other nation, left in a position where, on the west coast-it is almost as bad on the east coast-all these goods have to be carried in foreign vessels.


If there were Canadian ships, we would have some measure of control over the goods that were carried. It would be that much easier to get our own products carried abroad. It would be in the best interests of the nation as a whole. There may come a time, Mr. Speaker, when this government will even have to subsidize foreign vessels to come to our ports to carry Canadian goods abroad.
The figures on the merchant navy have made very sad reading for several years. They are growing steadily worse. I have here the seventh report of the Canadian maritime commission, dated June 24, 1954. We find at page 15 that in the year 1952 Canadian vessels carried only 6 * 4 per cent of Canada's trade; that was down from 20-2 per cent in 1947. United Kingdom vessels were carrying 35-4 per cent in 1952, which was down from 45-2 per cent in 1947. Other ships were carrying 58 * 2 per cent of our trade, whereas in 1947 they only carried 34-6 per cent. For 1953 the figures were worse. Then we only carried 4-3 per cent of our goods; the British carried 34 per cent and other vessels 61-7 per cent. I am sure that the figures for 1954, which have not yet been released, will be very much worse again.
We are down to the position where Canadian vessels are carrying practically none of Canada's products. The deep sea dry cargo fleet under the Canadian flag is practically gone. As I said, there are none left on the west coast. On January 1, 1948, there were 145 dry cargo vessels under Canadian registry. On December 31 of last year, there were only 15, two of them 10,000-tonners built during the war. One of these is Italian owned and operates out of ports in Italy. I believe it has not been in Canada for many years. There were seven 4,700-tonners, of which five belong to Canadian National Steamships and two are in the paper trade out of Newfoundland. Of the six others, three belong to the Canadian National Steamships and three are engaged in the coastal trade out of Newfoundland. Our gross tonnage has dropped from 928,598 tons on January 1, 1948, to 68,936 tons on December 31, 1954, the lowest point in 35 years. There are only about 500 Canadian merchant seamen. Almost every other nation has gone in the opposite direction.
I know there are certain ships under United Kingdom registry which are owned by Canadians but they are under United Kingdom direction and manned by United Kingdom sailors. They mean little to Canada and they are all old. Government policy is such that it prevents them from being modernized. We are told that Canada should rely on the North Atlantic Treaty Organization shipping

pool for its shipping; that if there is a war we will be served by that pool. There is no such pool in operation, and I understand that the United States is holding back; she has not agreed to come into the pool. If war were to come, Canada would have to start building all over again. There would be a great delay. There would be time required to train seamen, and a tremendous expenditure. It would probably be too late.
The government has had recommendation after recommendation from its own maritime commission and other officials that there should be a nucleus of approximately 50 modern fast vessels maintained for a Canadian merchant navy. But the policy adopted or the refusal to adopt any policy has resulted in this being one of the most dismal failures of the present government. I believe that even yet a bold policy could save the situation. I regret there is nothing about it in the speech from the throne.
My next subject concerns the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), who is a very good friend of mine and a minister for whom I have great admiration. Last session we asked if the government would help in the construction of the Marpole bridge over the north arm of the Fraser. I have not time to quote the Hansards; they are all here. I will not embarrass the minister by reading them. First he said no. Of course, the plea for help is based on the fact that this bridge is the only means of access to the Vancouver airport, wrach is the airport doing the most business in Canada. We pointed out that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) had said yes a few years ago. Eventually the Minister of Public Works, somewhat reluctantly, agreed that the government would pay $400,000.
That figure was reached on the basis of an estimate made some years ago that the way to repair this bridge was to put in a new span. The 6,000-odd vessels which go through every year would still be going through, and the span would still have to be opened for them. This government favoured improving the span, so he took the estimate of $1,200,000 for that job and said the government would pay one-third because it had been admitted that the dominion should pay one-third. We pointed out that was useless because there had to be a high level bridge. However, the minister would not raise the offer.
Finally on June 25 his parliamentary assistant had this to say in response to a question by myself, as reported on page 6774 of Hansard for that date:

No, that is after the election. Now, the bridge is not a revenue producing project; it will have to be a toll bridge, simply to pay the cost. I believe this is a case in which there still is an obligation on the dominion. The airport business is growing all the time; more money is to be spent on it by the dominion all the time. And the decision announced the other day -by the minister should be changed.
Finally I had meant to say a word in support of the establishment of the Canada council, but I do not have time to do so.
In closing may I give a friendly warning to the government. The Liberal party has been in office nearly twenty years, in five succeeding parliaments. In four of those parliaments that party has had an overwhelming majority. I am sure everyone here today who served in those five parliaments will agree that the one in which the sides were more evenly balanced was a far stronger parliament than any of the other four.
Watching those five governments, one can clearly see the government steadily growing more arrogant, with less and less reason. Today we have sign after sign that this government places very little importance on parliament, and more and more importance on the

The Address-Mr. Regier government itself. I suggest that we have, right here in this Liberal government-and not only among the cabinet ministers but also the private members-the greatest selfadmiration society in the whole country.

The manner in which the government has dealt with the questions to which I have referred this afternoon-unemployment, the Columbia river development, the price of wheat at Vancouver, the merchant navy and the Marpole bridge-and the reaction of the ministers when anyone dares to raise these questions, indicates clearly that their attitude is now becoming one of contempt for all contrary opinions.
Mind you, it is only human nature that when one has been in power, has been in command for such a long time, he thinks he is very good indeed. That is a natural human reaction. I can understand why members of the cabinet have that reaction-although I have noticed that while the older ones, who had some justification for it, go to jobs in different parts of the country, or retire, or go to the Senate, the younger ones who have just come up have the same sense of self-satisfaction that was held by men who really had some ground for it. That is one of the unfortunate features of the situation.
In any event, this government has been in power for a very long time. It would be a good thing for the country if there were a change. I merely point out to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that if there is a continuation of the attitude to which I have referred, then in the long run it will defeat the government. And, worse than that, it will result, as I believe it has already resulted, in the people of this country being given leadership which is far less efficient and far less democratic than they deserve.

Mr. Speaker, from the observations we have heard in the debate it would seem to be customary to hand out a lot of bouquets and congratulations when one rises to speak. However, I must say that I do not consider that in any way as part of my responsibility. I do not go even as far as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) when, in his closing remarks, he said that he wanted to offer some friendly advice to the government. My advice is designed deliberately to help the people of Canada get rid of what I consider has been the most reactionary government Canada has had since 1935. Therefore I have very few, if any, congratulations to offer.

The only congratulation I would extend would be to ask Mr. Deputy Speaker to transmit to Mr. Speaker our appreciation of the manner in which he has fulfilled his heavy responsibilities. Unlike the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), I can say honestly that in the province of British Columbia the man of French-Canadian descent from east of the Ottawa river who is considered most famous is the Speaker of the House of Commons, and not the gentleman who was referred to as "Uncle Louie". I might add that the prestige of the so-called "Uncle Louie" in British Columbia is very low, indeed.
It is often said in the house that this or that is the privilege of the opposition. That is a wrong process of thinking-very wrong. The opposition in the House of Commons has a responsibility, not a privilege. Whether we sit on the government or on the opposition side, we have the same privilege. Government members have one responsibility, that of governing the country according to their lights; and we definitely have the responsibility of seeing to it that, in face of the government majority, the people of Canada get the best possible government.
I am very pleased to speak in support of the amendment to the amendment of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I cannot see at all how the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) draws the conclusion that the leader of the C.C.F. was caught without his swimming trunks when the Progressive Conservative amendment was offered. That amendment follows the pattern of which we, in past years, may have been guilty-that of picking little individual items and castigating the government for not implementing them. Next year we have found they would implement them, and we would have to think of something new.
The time has arrived in the Canadian economic scene when little bits here and little remedies there are no longer sufficient. I agree wholeheartedly with my leader when he maintains that there is plenty of evidence to show that, by deliberate design, this government is turning itself from a genuinely Liberal government into a genuinely Conservative government.
I noticed that also in the address by the Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe). In years gone by it was the C.C.F. who told the government, "You are doing this and this. These are the things we have been asking for." This winter the C.C.F. are not going to be telling the government that they are doing the things we have been asking for. This winter, as we have already

heard in this house, the Acting Leader of the Opposition is going to be telling the government, "You are now intending to do the things the Conservative party of Canada has been advocating."
If you will look over the legislation that is proposed you will see that the Acting Leader of the Opposition has grounds for making that statement, and for claiming for the Tory party some of the credit. The time has arrived when a challenge is arising to the reactionary Liberal government headed by the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). The times are not too different from the years preceding the hungry 1930's. At that time the Canadian public was well aware that a complete switch in government policy was necessary. The only thing that was open to the Canadian public was to turn to the only alternative, the Conservative party. Now they have, under the guise of the Liberal party, a Conservative government, and this time there is an alternative available. From one end of Canada to the other, from Newfoundland to British Columbia, there is a genuine farmer-labour people's party that will be ready to take on the government of the country when an election again rolls around.
This government, in my opinion-and I think the speech from the throne shows plenty of evidence of that-is concerned only with the welfare of the Liberal party, and it is not doing very well at that. I notice that fewer than 14 per cent of the Canadian people have a Liberal party in office on the provincial level. Only the relatively smaller provinces of Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and Manitoba have Liberal regimes. Their fortunes are at a low ebb indeed.
When I was elected to this parliament one of the first things I made up my mind about was that I was going to get to know more about the country in which I live. I regret very much that the tour of the members of parliament to the province of British Columbia planned for last fall had to be postponed. I hope it has not been postponed for long, because I feel it is a great thing to be able to see how other people in Canada, thousands of miles away from us, live. I therefore spent a good deal of my summer and fall visiting other parts of Canada.
I should say the oftener I travel in Canada, the prouder I am of Canada. We have a wonderful nation, the most marvellous of all the nations of the world, and we have the most aggressive and progressive population. However, another impression I gathered that you cannot fail to notice is the vast
The Address-Mr. Regier potential, the vast possibilities that are open to the people of Canada. When one contemplates that one gets a certain feeling of humbleness and at times even of shame, when one sees all those natural resources and realizes how aggressive and sturdy the people are who are living here. That is particularly true when you realize we have such things as housing shortages, unemployment, lack of educational facilities, and so forth. The lack of aggressive action on the part of the Liberal government since 1935 in that respect has had a good deal to do with it.
I was in the maritimes, and I should like to congratulate the people there on having finally decided that their hope for help from a federal government that might be interested in the welfare of the whole nation was groundless. To look for help from such a federal government under this Liberal cabinet that we now have is to look in vain indeed; therefore these people have decided that they are going to see what they can do to help themselves. I welcome most heartily their formation of an interprovincial development council. I have not the exact name of it at my fingertips; however, I wish them well, and I hope this federal government may yet see fit to lend a hand, first of all in a reassessment, followed by a rehabilitation of the economic life of the whole of the maritimes.
The need to help themselves has of course long been evident in the province of Nova Scotia, where the people long ago realized that to look to the two old political parties for help in their difficulties was useless. They have led the whole of the maritime region in the formation of co-operatives and credit unions. However, in other parts of the maritimes I find that the people do not even realize what they have missed. They do not even seem to grasp the fact that the people of Canada are no longer living in the hungry thirties. When you see a new house in certain parts of New Brunswick you really lift up your head to look because it is something new, whereas in other parts of Canada new houses are a thing of almost everyday occurrence. If we could only take the people of New Brunswick on a tour from one end of Canada to the other; if they could see what is going on and how the people in Ontario, in Saskatchewan, in Alberta and in British Columbia are living, their high standard of living, I am sure they would decide that they had had enough of both Liberals and Conservatives.

I also spent a fair amount of time in the province of Quebec. This province seems to be the sore spot in the matter of Canadian unity. I was raised in the west. For years the late Mackenzie King told us how he was building national unity, and for years most of us believed him. "Yes, that is the man to build national unity." How is it, Mr. Speaker, if the late Mackenzie King was really and truly building national unity that, after such a long premiership, almost the moment he disappears from the scene we have less national unity than we have had in Canada for ages and ages?
One plea that I should like to make to the Prime Minister of Canada is this. I hope this house and the other house also will no longer be plagued with the necessity of sitting in a judicial capacity. We are here to legislate. I feel that a great opportunity may be missed if the present Prime Minister should want to resign, or because of circumstances of age or health have to resign, before this matter is settled. We do not want to handle divorce cases in the parliament of Canada.
At none of my meetings from one end of Canada to the other did I mention the subject of divorce; yet invariably, as soon as I sat down, the first thing I was asked was, "What about this question of divorce?" The people of Canada are getting sick and tired of it. There is one man who can help us out of this situation and that is the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I feel that if he does not do so he will have failed in one of his greater responsibilities.
It may interest my good Liberal friends who are hon. members of this house and who represent ridings in the province of Quebec to learn that when I came quite unannounced into the city of Montreal one day two clergymen of the Catholic faith, who somehow or other or by some unknown route had found out I was in Montreal, phoned me to ask for appointments. That was amazing to me. What did they want appointments for? They wanted to know the story from other than Liberal sources for a change. They wanted to get at the root of the difficulty and the dissatisfaction. Not only that; one of them referred a number of cases to me and pleaded with me to take up the fight on behalf of people whom he felt might be injured. I assured him that I hoped not to have to do that and that a solution would be found to remove this business from parliament.
I have received numerous letters from outside Quebec. I have received letters from


the Riviera and the Scandinavian countries, from former Canadians whose lives had been so messed up by their cases having been handled in the houses of parliament of Canada that they felt obligated to remove themselves from Canada and spend the rest of their lives elsewhere. I think it is a shame that we are not able to end this matter once and for all. At this time I make this plea to the Prime Minister, that he do what he can. If he cannot do anything I doubt whether there is any future Liberal prime minister who will be able to do anything. He would have to be a resident of Ontario, because such a man could not possibly come from western Canada.
Another matter that worries the people of Canada a great deal, and that excites a lot of interest, is this knight in shining armour who was once and for all going to rid the political scene of Canada of a certain man. He was to rid us of him politically speaking; we wish him well personally. I am referring to the premier of Quebec. I am told that assurance was given last winter to the Liberal members of parliament from Quebec somewhat along these lines: "Now, boys, you stay with me in this fight. When it is over and we have won our fight in the house I will put on this armour and go out and do personal battle, and we will end up on top."
The guns were fired, but what happened? I wonder how those Liberal members of parliament who put their faith in the Prime Minister feel about it now. They must be most humiliated indeed, because from all appearances the premier of Quebec seems to have won a complete victory. All he did was this. When he got a slap on one cheek he turned the other cheek, and the Prime Minister of Canada had to humiliate the whole nation by boarding a train to go to meet the master of that other nation in a hotel room in Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext: Does the hon. member know of any declaration made by the head of any government in this country which was more widely approved or more universally commended throughout Canada than the speech made by the Prime Minister of Canada at the Reform club in Quebec?

That is exactly what I am saying. All Canada looked forward with great anticipation, the progressive people in the province of Quebec looked forward with great anticipation to the political battle which was shaping up on the Canadian scene. Then there was the utter humiliation and shame that all of us felt when it ended up in a complete turnabout in this hotel room in Montreal.
The people of Quebec are going to wake up. There are enough of them to turn the

tide. My forecast is that when that tide turns in the province of Quebec it is going to turn mighty fast. My greatest concern is that it may turn to the communist party. I contend that there is no part of Canada that is as ripe for advances by the communist party as the province of Quebec. In the city of Montreal the communist party polled about as many votes as the C.C.F.
