subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I think I am safe in saying that I have spent more days in the province of Quebec than any six members of parliament from Quebec taken together have spent in British Columbia.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I should like the hon. member to answer that question. How many days did he spend in the province of Quebec when he went there last summer?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have not added them up; I do not know the number of days I was there last summer. The people of Quebec are suffering. They are subjected to double taxation and they are not enjoying the facilities in the field of education which they would like to have, which they ought to have and which they deserve as Canadian citizens. They are not receiving adequate health services to which they are entitled. I was amazed to learn that it was many years after the rest of Canada was enjoying old age pensions before Quebec was granted this privilege. One reason for this was that when the late Mr. Mackenzie King, while leader of the Liberal party, was preaching national unity, on the other side of the Ottawa river he was telling the people of Quebec, "You are something apart; you are something different; you must have special consideration."
I regret to admit that all the political parties of Canada represented in the province of Quebec are of one accord. They are all supporters, consciously or otherwise, of the basic philosophy of the premier of Quebec.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Wishful thinking.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is not wishful thinking. I have seen resolutions passed by the Quebec branches of various political parties. I have said to the people of Montreal, and they applauded me when I said it, that unity in Canada cannot be based on anything except the needs of the people. Human beings in Montreal are the same as human beings in Winnipeg or in any other Canadian city. The people of Canada want decent housing and decent food. They want employment. They want health services. We all want these things whether we live in one part of Canada or another. There is your basis of unity for
The Address-Mr. Regier the Canadian people. The C.C.F. is the only party which has arisen out of the needs of the people of Canada and is therefore able to tell the same story in all parts of Canada.
If hon. members do not like what I have been saying about the province of Quebec we will go to the next province, the province of Ontario. In the province of Ontario I found widespread complaints about the administration of the Department of National Revenue. I was told by civil servants that it is the worst administered department of the government of Canada. The customs officers along the line do not seem to know where they are at. One makes one ruling one day and another one comes in the next day and overrules that, making a different regulation. I think it is time for a complete overhaul, and I say this in all kindness to the minister for I believe he should do this before he leaves that department, possibly to take on another. He should order a complete reassessment such as we had with the Criminal Code last year. I believe it is time the regulations of the Department of National Revenue were consolidated and the difficulties ironed out. However, we will have more of that later in the session.
There is a great housing shortage, and in this regard I was interested to hear the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) state that N.H.A. houses are being built for $10,000. The hon. member mentioned a down payment of $1,500, and I earnestly hope homes are available at that figure. However, I would like to be reassured on that point and know for certain that the people of Toronto who are eligible for N.H.A. homes can buy a $10,000 home for a down payment of $1,500.
The people of Ontario are worried about the question of immigration, especially as it relates to unemployment. We fail to understand how so many individual applicants for immigration into Canada can be turned down, yet wherever we go in the major centres of Canada there seem to be hundreds of single immigrants who have come into this country and are now without employment. It has long been suspected that the department of immigration, either deliberately or through lack of planning and direction, is allowing thousands of single workers into Canada, people with no contacts in Canada and possibly only the promise of short-time employment, while keeping out others whom we ought to welcome into our country. I shall not go into detail on that because of lack of time.
In the province of Manitoba the record speaks for itself. I was amazed at the efforts the Liberal party made to win the Selkirk

The Address-Mr. Regier by-election. I understand one cabinet minister was sent in for a repeat performance. If he had been sent in once more the Liberal candidate might actually have lost his deposit. I also understand that 48 hours before the voters went to the polls they were told that the so-called payment on wheat would be 10 cents a bushel, and it would be paid out shortly after the by-election.
I would like to congratulate whoever is in charge of the Liberal party organization in Canada, for under his guidance the party made a tremendous effort to bolster their rapidly sinking prestige in the province of Manitoba. However, Manitoba is a little more progressive than a great many other parts of Canada. To the Liberal party I would say, "Your cause in Manitoba is completely hopeless. In addition, it will require another five to ten years before you begin to grow again in British Columbia, while in Alberta there is no hope for you at all, and even less in Saskatchewan. Your efforts to hold Manitoba will be completely fruitless."
I spent a good deal of time in Saskatchewan, and I found the people there taking this terrible trimming over the crop failure in their usual manner. However, they are bitterly disappointed over the failure of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to come through with the dam. The yarn going around Saskatchewan is that the Minister of Agriculture has made up his mind that before he leaves the political scene he is going to do everything he can to obtain the dam, and thus not go down in history as a political failure. In fact, we are told in Saskatchewan that at every cabinet meeting all the Minister of Agriculture speaks about is the dam, and the other cabinet ministers are getting to the point where they say, "Damn the Minister of Agriculture, damn the dam, and damn all Saskatchewan anyhow".
Then we come to the province of Alberta, and there we find a rather fluid situation in regard to political life. The people there are rapidly becoming disillusioned with their present government, particularly when they see a clergyman, a humble servant of the people, placed in charge of one of the most important government departments and end up, after leaving the political scene, as the head of a company which threatens to become one of the biggest private utility companies in Canada. When they see that they begin to wonder.
The government there promised to do away with all tax on land, but taxes on land have been gradually rising despite the fact that hundreds of millions of dollars of oil revenue

has gone into the provincial coffers. In the light of these facts the people cannot understand why their taxes continue to increase.
We have not a Liberal organization in Alberta worthy of the name. We have some Liberal members in the legislature, but they have no organization behind them. I would point out, though, that the C.C.F. in Alberta has a vital, wide-awake, active organization, and the leader of the Social Credit party might get the shock of his life before six more months have passed. In fact, we might have to rearrange the seating in this house before very long.
Coming now to the province of British Columbia, which might be described as the garden of Eden-I had "paradise" in my notes but I had to change that because of our present government there and because I remembered, Mr. Speaker, that the garden of Eden was not a perfect place; there was an influence there. However, coming back to British Columbia I believe that politically it has made greater advances than any other province in Canada in that we have finally consolidated a two-party system. Hon. members might take a look at today's Hansard and read how the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green) made a powerful plea on behalf of the rights of the provincial government in British Columbia. His was nothing more than an attempt to get that government off the hook in its fight over power with the federal government, which it is rapidly losing.
They were elected as the free enterprise party. They told the farmers there that the reason they were not getting more for their milk was because the government was intervening in the milk situation. They told people in the urban areas, "You are paying too much for your milk. Take the government out of the milk business. Government in business is a bad thing. It is Marxian and basically bad." The farmers and the urban dwellers fell for it, but I am still paying 22 cents per quart for my milk. Farmers in the Fraser valley of British Columbia have lost untold hundreds of thousands of dollars as a result of this policy, and now they are beginning to worry about it. They have managed to get a commission appointed and the "Socreds" are worrying about how they can save face and again sneak back into the milk business.
I was pleased to note that apparently the leader of the Social Credit party pleaded yesterday for orderly marketing for farm produce. Last year I was also pleased to hear him speak in favour of abolishing tolls on bridges. I hope that he can somehow

exercise some restraint and stop the wild antics of those who are nothing but smart-aleck politicians, who lead a rather reluctant Social Credit group in the house in Victoria.
Then we have the new Conservative party there, and it has a most useful role to play. I have no objection to the Conservative party. I have every admiration for it. It has a necessary part to play in a democracy. It is the party of consolidation, while the C.C.F. party is the party of progress. Let the Conservative party now call itself "Socred" or even "Union Nationale". It is immaterial, and it is all right with me. It has a political function to perform. However, what I do object to is this Liberal party that is neither here nor there, that is not a free enterprise party and is not socialistically inclined. It is based on nothing, I repeat, except the welfare of the Liberal party. That will come to an end when economic circumstances change and the people demand a government that believes in action. They will either elect the right wing or the left wing, and I can forecast a split right down the middle in the membership across the way.
Who the new leader of the right wing will be I do not know. I hear that sparring for the position is going on, and that a number of very aggressive and fairly young individuals are concerned. It is my firm conviction that the Liberal party in British Columbia has disappeared as a political force. The main reason, I am verily beginning to believe, is that the bottom of the Fraser river is paved with the gold and studded with the diamonds of Liberal political patronage. We had a Fraser river gold rush many years ago, and it is said that history has a way of repeating itself. This patronage and pork barrel politics were the main reason for the wiping out of the Liberal government in Saskatchewan, and this also holds true for the province of British Columbia. There is an answer to the situation. The people do not know what is going on and the opposition, apparently, has no place in government. I sometimes wonder if we have any place. I sometimes even wonder why the private Liberal members of parliament sitting around and behind the cabinet ministers are here at all. They have no influence on the government, and I do not know why they are here.
This Canada of ours is definitely ruled by a cabinet that has all the facilities at its command to defend its position, right or wrong. I fully endorse the plea made by the Conservatives some time ago, about which I read in the newspapers, that greater facilities be made available to the opposition members so
The Address-Mr. Regier they can do their work properly. When I referred to the Fraser river you might think that I exaggerated. Maybe I did, but how am I to know? What means are available to me to find out whether or not the half a million dollars for this project and the $2 million for that project are a waste of money?
When the cabinet wants to defend its position with regard to expenditures on certain public works it has all research facilities available. The matter has become so serious that after the last election there were articles in certain newspapers pointing out that Canada was beginning to have a one-party government. To anyone who has sat in the galleries of the house over a period of years I think it must be very obvious that we are rapidly approaching the day, if this situation carries on much longer and opposition members are unable to do too much about it, when not only will we have a bipartisan foreign policy, as we sometimes do, but all our policies will be bipartisan, and that would be a sad day for the cause of democracy.
I should like to endorse what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) with regard to the trans-Canada highway and the assumption of responsibility by the federal government for all major highways in Canada. I think the time is long overdue when municipal and provincial taxpayers should be afforded some measure of relief from the burden of taxation brought about by road construction and maintenance. Money is so urgently needed for municipal development that we cannot longer afford to see so much of the income of the lower levels of government being used for road building.
I should like also to advocate that a committee of the house be established, or even a royal commission, to investigate all expenditures of the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production since the end of the war. I think the most amazing information would be revealed. That is another place where the opposition is handicapped. I would say that even the Liberal members who are not in the cabinet are severely handicapped in fulfilling their function in the house. I know that the Department of National Defence has wasted $300,000 in my riding in the purchase of a swamp, land that is absolutely useless for the purpose for which it was bought. Somebody made a mistake. I am not saying that the government must necessarily be condemned for a mistake, but they spent $300,000 for land on which to build an army supply depot, and the land turned out to have no bottom to it. At least, no bottom has been found so far, and the land is most unsuited for that purpose.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising on this occasion to speak on behalf of my constituents I am sure they would want me to convey to you and to the members of the house their best wishes for the coming year. I should also like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I also congratulate the new members of parliament for giving up all those things with which they were occupied previous to coming here and giving of themselves to the nation's business.
Naturally there were some disappointments last year, but as we look back we have reason to believe that there was much for which to be thankful. Many of our disappointments were brought about by things beyond our control. Weather conditions in the part of my riding where I live were very bad so far as the production of logs and lumber is concerned. Across Canada we find that conditions for agriculture were anything but good.
Dealing with British Columbia, and more particularly with the riding of Cariboo in which I am most interested, we find it is expected that tenders will be called for the Dawson Creek federal building early this year. For a good many years we have been looking forward to the construction of this building, and I am certain that the people of that area appreciate a great deal the action that is being taken this year.
Whilst speaking in connection with the Dawson Creek area, I should like to mention that we are pleased to hear that the telephone situation will be cleared up within the next 18 months, and that a dial system will be introduced in Dawson Creek. I should like to recommend at this time, in connection with improvements in the Dawson Creek area, that an unattended automatic set-up for Pouce Coupe be considered, which would give a 24-hour service from that town into the central point of Dawson Creek.
I should like to congratulate the government on the appointment of the new Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) because I believe that, as well as having great ability, he has many other admirable qualities. We are looking forward to seeing some good results from his department.


The provincial government of British Columbia has contributed a great deal to the welfare of our people. Among the things that interest me most is the extension of the Pacific Great Eastern from Squamish to Vancouver. This extension, as you perhaps know, is well under way. It is expected that the extension from Prince George to Fort St. John will be under way next year. I understand that tenders for the construction of the first 65 miles will be called some time early in February.
As a result of the confidence in the British Columbia government there has been a great deal of private investment throughout the whole province. This sometimes brings with it circumstances which cause the government a bit of concern. Because of the rapid expansion, the educational facilities in the province, as elsewhere in Canada, can hardly keep pace with the growth in population.
In the northern part of my constituency there is an increased interest in gas and oil exploration. The proposed gas line from Fort St. John to Vancouver and to the inland empire of the Pacific northwest in the United States brings a great deal of hope for our people throughout the length and breadth of the Cariboo riding because we expect many new secondary industries will be brought into being.
I noticed that in the Vancouver Sun of January 3, in speaking about this development, Frank Walden, who is a staff writer for the Vancouver Sun had this to say:
The year 1954 was as action-packed from a Social Credit government's point of view, as the violent election years of 1952 and 1953. The shouting was not perhaps as loud, but more, in fact a good deal, was accomplished.
Again on the economic side, I may say that British Columbia bonds sold for the highest price ever in the eastern money markets. Frobisher posted with the government a colossal $2,500,000 bond and prepared to build an immense hydrochemical empire in the northern section of British Columbia. Alcan announced another $45 million expansion program ahead of schedule. There is every reason for the people of British Columbia to be optimistic, and we expect that as time goes on a much greater development will take place within the province.
The point I should like to make at this time is that all these developments are going to add substantially to the federal government's revenues. Under the tax agreements we find that the greater the development, naturally the more money the federal government is going to collect. We feel, therefore, that there are certain responsibilities the federal government must meet in connection

with collecting that additional revenue from British Columbia. We would expect the federal government to take steps to assist the province to continue this rapid development in order that the people of Canada including those of British Columbia may enjoy a higher standard of living and a greater Canada.
The people of British Columbia are active and enterprising, and are much encouraged by the sound policy of the British Columbia government, which is noted for being a government that talks less and does more. That this feeling of optimism is growing there is no doubt. We do feel that there should be no encroachment upon provincial rights by the federal government in anything that is done.
Speaking last session regarding transportation facilities I mentioned the highway problem, as recorded at page 180 of Hansard for November 19, 1953. But before dealing with the problem of highways, I should like to mention one matter of interest not only to the people in that part of British Columbia from which I come but also to all the people of Canada. We find we have a situation in which there are two large Canadian railroads being subsidized by the taxpayers of Canada. These subsidies put the railways in a position where they can set rates without regard to whether or not they lose money. As long as the railways are being subsidized, there is no reason why the railway company could not carry freight for nothing in order to meet competition.
The trucking problem has been brought to my attention, and the position of the trucking company is becoming hopeless. It might be said by some that the trucking business is being subsidized, but I think that is a long way from the truth. The trucking industry pays a tax of 10 cents per gallon on gasoline and licence fees for the use of the highways. These highways are needed for the lighter traffic as well as for heavy loads on the short hauls on which the railways are not able to give service.
I should like to quote some figures which are very revealing in connection with freight rates and agreed charges. I find that according to the Canadian freight classification there is a fourth class rate of $2.98 against an agreed charge of $2.09, which is being charged for first class freight. I see that the first class freight rate is $5.04, according to the Canadian freight classification. These figures speak for themselves. Again referring to the figures we see that from Edmonton to McBride, a distance of 350 miles, the second class freight rate is $2.26. From Vancouver to Dawson Creek, a distance of 1,400 miles, the first class freight rate under agreed charges
The Address-Mr. Leboe is $2.09, or 17 cents less to bring freight 1,400 miles than to take the same freight 350 miles, where there is no trucking competition. I think this situation is grossly unfair and demands the immediate attention of the government.
The whole rate problem must be brought under review. There is no doubt in the world that in a pioneering country especially-and perhaps I need not say "especially"-this is necessary. I am familiar particularly with that part of the trucking industry which serves the constituency of Cariboo. I know that many hundreds of miles of that constituency are served only by trucking. If we have a situation where subsidized railways can cut the rates and take the long hauls away from that trucking industry, it will throw it into a position where it cannot take care of local freight, either. We need the trucking industry, and we must do something to protect it from the ravages of subsidized railways that can cut rates down to nothing, if necessary-because it makes no difference to them, so long as the taxpayer is going to meet the difference, in the final analysis.
I come now to a matter which has been discussed by at least four members so far at this session, and that is the question of federal participation in the construction of arterial highways. I believe that so long as the federal government is collecting the bulk of the taxes from the people in the provinces of Canada, more should be done in connection with the highways. As I said before, this could be linked with the defence program. I believe the time has come when the government should take a close look at the highway situation in Canada, particularly in the light of what is going on in our neighbouring country to the south. We find that United States expenditures planned for the next number of years amount to more than $100 billion. In addition they have planned for $8 billion to be spent on toll roads for the northern and central parts of that country.
In view of the great extension of the roads they already have in that country-and the roads now going to be built are termed as necessary, I understand, under the defence program-we in Canada must surely realize that we are falling far behind in our program of road building. I noticed in an editorial in the Edmonton Journal of November 3, 1954, a heading "Military Loads and Roads." One paragraph in the editorial states:
Last year, provincial highways minister Gordon Taylor requested federal aid in the construction of what would be military traffic arteries in this province. He said that the provinces should not be expected to build highways which would carry heavy military traffic in the event of an attack on
!26	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Leboe this country. Such traffic would require roads of a very high standard of construction to ensure mobility. The federal government rejected this request when it was made in concert by the western provinces. Nevertheless, it has been apprised of the situation in warnings by Colonel J. R. B. Jones, chief engineer of the Canadian army, of the general inadequacy of Canadian highways for military requirements.
Hon. George Prudham is opposed to construction of military highways outward from Edmonton as he does not think they will ever be needed for such use. It would be well for him to seek instruction from experts of the defence department on this vital subject.
I would not feel justified in stressing the need for highways so much were it not for the fact that we realize the development of any country depends upon its highway and transportation facilities. I would urge this government to take another look at the whole highways situation with a view to providing more aid to the provinces in that regard.
In this connection we do not advocate an increase in the national debt to do the job. I believe the Bank of Canada could be made a bank of issue; and the Bank of Canada as a bank of issue could monetize our national liquid assets, part of the difference between national income and national production. By so doing, without increasing the national debt and without necessarily paying any interest on the money issued, it could bring about a situation where surplus consumer goods not being bought today could be put into the hands of the unemployed. Those people could be set to work to build these badly needed highways. In this way there would be no increase in the national debt. We would only be using liquid assets we already have in the form of consumer goods.
This could apply, of course, to many other phases of government. At the moment I think particularly of our senior citizens and all the other recipients of social assistance who are so badly in need of help, which situation we all recognize.
We have heard a good deal about the unemployment situation, and I am not going to say much about it. However, I do go along with those who advocate bringing about a situation in Canada where we do not have to give out supplementary benefits, but who urge rather that we have a situation under which those who want to work would have the opportunity to do so. We know this is a young country and that there is much to do. We know we have the machines to do it; we have the manpower. Therefore there is no reason in the world why, with the manpower and the machines, the work could not be done, since we have the liquid assets in the form of consumer goods that need to be consumed.


The government of British Columbia took action in connection with the unemployment situation in that province, taking the position that if the federal government was not going to give assistance, then the provincial government would not see the people left without the means of livelihood.
One feature that affects my constituency particularly is that contracts for part of the construction on the Pacific Great Eastern Railway have been brought forward three or four months so that by the spring breakup in the lumbering industry in the Prince George area the work will be getting under way, so as to relieve the unemployment situation during the spring lay-off period. These are situations in which the government is active in looking after its people, and I feel very certain that they are going a long way in their policies to bring about better federal and provincial relations.
We must give more autonomy to the provinces rather than putting the autonomy all in the federal government. We must get back to bringing the government closer to the people so the people of this land will have a closer contact with the government, and therefore be able to let their voices be heard much more often than in the past. We must get back to the position where people can get their needs before the government. The further away we get from the municipal and provincial level the harder it is going to be for the people of Canada to get any action on problems that require government attention.
I do not want to speak too long. In closing I wish to say that I was interested to note that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam (Mr. Regier) was attempting to pick to pieces, as it were, the British Columbia government. I should like to remind him that for 17 years or so the C.C.F. were in opposition, but the people of British Columbia turned them down at the polls when the time came to elect a government other than the Liberal government that was in power at that time.

Mr. Speaker, I too want to congratulate the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) and to add my welcome to the new members who were elected at the by-elections last fall.
I of course am a member from what the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) described as a backward province, namely New Brunswick, in which he said a new house was a rarity. I am sure the places he visited would not be at all

pleased to hear him say that today; and I can assure him, even without visiting his riding, that we have more new houses in Westmorland county than he has in his riding, because last year he rose in his place in this house during a debate on housing and said that many people in his riding were living in tarpaper shacks, to which at the time the hon. member for Burnaby-Rich-mond (Mr. Goode) objected.
I had intended to say something during my speech about the dredging of a harbour down in New Brunswick, Pointe du Chene harbour, which is part of my responsibility. However, the hon. member, who conducted one of the quickest national surveys I have ever heard of, took it upon himself to take an interest in that harbour in Westmorland county, New Brunswick. I should like to read an extract from the Moncton Transcript of June 23, 1954:
Erhart Regier, C.C.F. member of parliament for Burnaby-Coquitlam, British Columbia, in a two-day speaking tour of Westmorland county was critical of the Liberal government and what he calls "their do-nothing" attitude.
Speaking last night at Sackville and the evening before at Petitcodiac Mr. Regier referred to the needed dredging of Point du Chene channel and charged that the government would do nothing until pressed by united action from several directions.
I have pressed for the dredging of that channel from one direction. That is all I can do. I was looking forward at this session to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam pressing for it from several directions; but apparently since leaving Westmorland he has lost interest in the dredging of this channel. The newspaper report of his speech goes on to say:
He said that the people of British Columbia would be pleased to see federal funds spent on the rehabilitation of the maritime economic life as they realize that the prosperity of Canada as a whole depended on the well-being of all parts of the nation.
In that regard he apparently is speaking for the government of British Columbia. Today he was not a bit satisfied with the way the government of British Columbia was running that province. I was startled to hear him pick apart the Social Credit government, particularly after speaking for them. I can also tell him that in New Brunswick the people sometimes do change their minds politically. They did that a year or two ago and elected a Progressive Conservative government. However, since the C.C.F. party was organized in New Brunswick their vote has steadily declined. In Westmorland county the last candidate received about half as many votes as he did four years previously. Socialism in Westmorland county is definitely on its way out.

At the last session I spoke on the Chignecto canal, or the eastern extension of the St. Lawrence seaway. As has been suggested, it can be properly called the eastern passage. I intend to deal with this matter again today, but before I do so I should like to mention other matters which as the representative of Westmorland county I have been asked to bring to the attention of the house.
Firstly, in the centre of Westmorland county is the largest railway centre east of Montreal. It is the headquarters for the Atlantic division, and it is where the repair shops are located. The economic life of my district reacts quickly to any changes in the Canadian National Railways, that is to say, any increase or decrease in the staff of the Canadian National Railways, Atlantic division. To us in New Brunswick this transportation system is more than a business to be run on a profit and loss basis as private enterprise. Separated as we are from the rest of Canada by the state of Maine, it means that we have to travel through an entire state of a foreign country, or around it, to do business with the rest of the Dominion of Canada.
The Canadian National Railways is a public utility, and therefore cannot be considered in relation to the province of New Brunswick in the same light as a private enterprise. The repair shops in Moncton repair and manufacture parts for the entire system, and for a number of years the entire economy of my constituency has been built around these shops. It is most unfair to reduce the staff because of a change-over from steam locomotives to diesels. These tradesmen have been put out of work, and there is no other industry in that locality to which they can turn for employment.
I have been asked by the union representatives in Moncton to protest the lay-offs in the Atlantic region. This request has been made
128	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. H. J. Murphy also by the Canadian National war veterans' association.	I am more than pleased to
endorse their stand. I suggest that there should be an investigation into the Atlantic region of the Canadian National Railways in an effort to find a means of providing full employment for the railway workers in the maritimes.
Since I spoke last in this house urging the construction of a Chignecto canal or eastern passage, many organizations and citizens have asked that the construction of this canal be started at once. Last summer the maritimes marine workmen's federation, meeting in Sydney, adopted a resolution calling upon the governments of the four Atlantic provinces to demand that the federal government make an immediate start on the construction of a Chignecto canal across the isthmus between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Last summer the New Brunswick federation of labour, meeting in Bathurst, New Brunswick, asked for the immediate construction of this isthmus project. The union of municipalities, representing every city, town and county in the entire province of New Brunswick, unanimously supported by resolution the construction of a Chignecto canal. In addition to the groups I have mentioned there are 80-odd other organizations which have endorsed this project.
In September, 1954, the Maritime Advocate published an article which would seem to be a boiling down of the sentiments of the citizens of the district in relation to the construction of a Chignecto canal. This reads:
It strikes me that it is now or never so far as the Chignecto canal is concerned. The St. Lawrence seaway, which will undoubtedly be detrimental to the Atlantic provinces, is going ahead no matter what happens. It is up to the federal government to construct the Chignecto canal which will do a great deal to allay the fears of maritime people that the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway will prove a big setback for the Atlantic provinces. Now is the time for all the federal members from Atlantic provinces to stand together, irrespective of party politics. It is now or never. If there is not concerted action in favour of the construction of the Chignecto canal now then we in the Atlantic provinces may as well give up the fight and stand with our hands out, praying for a few nickels from the wealthy tables of the central provinces.
In addition I have been sent a copy of a resolution adopted at the 54th annual meeting of the maritime provinces board of trade, reading as follows:
Whereas, during the last session, the Minister of Transport of the federal government expressed his views in the House of Commons that a study should be made into the feasibility of the construction of the Chignecto canal; and
Whereas, it is considered that the construction of the Chignecto canal could be linked with the development of electric power through utilization of bay


of Fundy tides and that this development could produce abundant low cost power which would greatly enhance the opportunity of attracting industries to these maritime provinces,
Therefore, be it resolved: that the maritime provinces board of trade, assembled in session at Halifax, Nova Scotia, this 4th day of October, 1954, urge the government of Canada to investigate at the earliest possible moment the feasibility of the construction of the Chignecto canal, at the same time keeping in mind the possibility of power development as an allied phase of any such construction.
Also in the same month the Atlantic regional employment committee of the unemployment insurance commission is reported in the Saint John Tele graph-Journal of August 29 as having passed a resolution in connection with the Chignecto canal, reading as follows:
The second resolution pointed out that a canal through the isthmus of Chignecto would prove "highly beneficial" to the maritime provinces and greatly expanding national economy.
Benefits of such a canal would be toward greater national defence, faster ocean communication and speedier means of shipping, the resolution continued.
"Creation of a canal piercing the Chignecto isthmus would seem complementary to the St. Lawrence and great lakes development now being undertaken by the federal government", the resolution said.
Points in favour of the canal are, according to the resolution, possibility of a number of starting points for convoys, greater ability on the part of the "western allies" to dispatch convoys from different points on the eastern Canadian coast, and effective deterrent to aggression and inevitable influence to Canadian and American industry by the mineral discoveries of the Ungava peninsula and Bathurst area.
The resolution declared also that advocates in the United States of the Passamaquoddy power development "have definitely maintained for some time that a Chignecto canal would have influence on industrial development in the Atlantic coast section of New England."
Last year I traced the history of the Chignecto canal back over a period of about 300 years. I pointed out that promises had been made by former governments. There had been times in our history when the construction of the Chignecto canal seemed to be very certain, but in the past not too much has been said about the power aspects of the Chignecto canal. It might be likened to the St. Lawrence seaway which is said to be a water route from central Canada to other countries of the world; but the consequent development of power which would be available to the central provinces is most important.
We in New Brunswick need cheap power. I believe a by-product of the construction of a Chignecto canal, if properly planned, would be a block of power which would improve the economic condition of our area. There have been many routes suggested for the canal, all of which are practical, but I am

not concerned so much with the route as with the acceptance of the principle of the construction of a canal to pierce the isthmus.
The construction of this canal would provide a short route in sheltered waters to the trading points in the bay of Fundy and in New England for the products of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. It would increase coastwise shipping between the gulf of St. Lawrence, the bay of Chaleur, Northumberland strait and the bay of Fundy. It would increase regular steamship sailings between the Atlantic provinces and central Canada. A Chignecto canal would make it convenient for vessels plying between Montreal and points on the Atlantic seaboard to call at ports not only in the bay of Fundy but in northern Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and northern New Brunswick, and enable them to load or discharge cargoes and passengers. It would revive native industries which flourished years ago, and it would create a new economy in the Atlantic provinces.
It may surprise many residents of Canada to know that four years after confederation the percentage of population employed in industry in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick, was almost equal to the percentage of population similarly employed in Quebec and Ontario. Seventy-five years later, however, a tremendous change took place. Ontario and Quebec had been steadily enriched and their industrial employment average rose. In the Atlantic provinces there had not been an increase but a devastating decline. Incidentally, in that period New Brunswick dropped from first place to fourth among the five provinces.
Prior to confederation the maritime provinces were regarded as the most prosperous in British North America. New Brunswick, on a per capita basis, was the most industrialized of any of the provinces then comprising Canada. The lack of a Chignecto canal is one of the reasons our prosperity and industrial development have lagged far behind Quebec and Ontario. In 1871, of every five Canadian industrial workers, one was employed in the maritimes. In 1946 the ratio had dropped to one out of every 17. Again, in 1871 the industrial wage paid to the worker in New Brunswick was the highest in Canada. In 1946 that province had almost the lowest wage rate in Canada.
Besides the tremendous saving in shipping distances, the building of the canal would mean that many of the present small ports would be developed to carry on both a coastwise and an ocean-going business. The 50433-9
The Address-Mr. H. J. Murphy time then has come, after many attempts over the past 300 years, for the government to fulfil its confederation promise and build the Chignecto canal.
Before closing there is one other matter I would like to bring to the attention of the house, for it is a matter of serious concern to us in New Brunswick. That is the plight of our farmers. It is true that we have many successful farmers outside our larger towns and cities, most of them specializing in daily farm products such as liquid milk for the supply of these centres. But if you drive through Westmorland county and some of the adjoining counties you will see many abandoned farms with windows in the houses boarded up and the place left to rot. That is a terrible situation, and I would like to know of some way in which to remedy it. We have, of course, a Canadian farm loan board, but apparently that was designed more to assist the farmers of western and central Canada, and in my opinion it is not suited to the purpose of assisting the farmers in New Brunswick. To the best of my knowledge there was only one Canadian farm loan board application granted in Westmorland county last year. I may be wrong, but certainly there were not more than three or four.
In this connection I would like to point out, and it should be recognized in the regulations, that there are other types of farming in addition to those known in central and western Canada. In New Brunswick a man could have a farm close to the sea and during a few weeks of the year he could go down to the shore line and fish. This would provide him with a small cash income. In another district a farmer may have a wood lot at the back of his farm from which he cuts a certain amount of wood each year, in fact probably the same amount as his father and grandfather cut in their day. Out of that small supply of wood he makes another small cash income. In addition, part of his farm may be composed of rocky land on which nothing grows very well except small spruce and fir trees. Each year in the fall he thins them out for the Christmas tree trade. In fact in New Brunswick this has become quite an industry, and I am told that last fall nearly 10 million trees were shipped from that province.
The point I wish to make is that a farmer may farm his wood lot, he may farm his spruce and fir trees for the Christmas trade, or he may fish along the edge of his farm, but it appears that this type of farming is not to be recognized under the regulations

I shall not take up the time of the house to mention the many benefits we have received which have been provided by the Liberal party for the people of New Brunswick, but I do want to mention in closing that we are not as poor or as hard up as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam made out earlier today.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, not because it has become a customary practice to do so, but because of the excellent manner in which they acquitted themselves on Friday last.
We have been told that the hon. member for Verdun has an outstanding background as a scholar and a jurist in his native province. Those of us who come from the province of Ontario know the member for Trinity as a prominent athlete, an outstanding scholar and a notable member of the bar of this province. I am sure that both these members will represent the people of their constituencies in a manner that will do credit to themselves and to the provinces from which they come.
The past twelve months have brought many new obligations to Canada in the sphere of international affairs. Canada has assumed the responsibility of endeavouring to work out a satisfactory armistice in Indo-China during the past six months. Our representatives have attended conferences in London and Paris in order to bring about a European alliance and unite the countries of western Europe. We in Canada endeavoured to be a genial host to representatives who came to this country in connection with the Colombo plan conference. In all these projects our delegations have contributed their sincere and faithful efforts to maintain peace among men of good will.
It is traditional that representatives who come here and the people of Canada generally think very much alike as to what our position should be in the matter of international affairs. During the past summer I had the honour of being one of the delegation that attended the commonwealth parliamentary conference in Nairobi. One of the things noticeable there was that our delegates, regardless of their political affiliations
[Air. Alurphy (Westmorland).]

in Canada, all thought alike as far as the fundamentals of freedom, security and humanity were concerned. The Canadian people expect us to show the same united front in opposition to tyranny, oppression and aggression in dealing with international matters in this house. Canada is united at the present time as never before in her history in those things which are most important to the people of this country. This state of union in our country reflects credit on the wisdom, foresight and veracity of our national leaders both past and present.
The present administration has been responsible in the past for many measures of social reform, so it is not surprising to me to see reflected in the speech from the throne certain refinements to many of these social reforms. We must admit that there are certain patches of unemployment throughout the country. These matters require attention, and the people of Canada will be glad to know that amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act are being introduced this session at the earliest possible moment. These amendments will provide a measure of relief for those people who are unemployed. The scale of supplementary payments will be placed on a par with regular payments. Labour organizations throughout the country are looking forward to a general overhaul, as forecast, of the Unemployment Insurance Act itself.
As one of the members of the veterans affairs committee of this house, I was proud to learn that certain amendments were being introduced at this session dealing with the war veterans allowance. Veterans' groups throughout the country will welcome these proposed amendments. With the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan), I attended meetings of veterans' groups in the Niagara peninsula before coming here. I am sure these groups are not asking for the ultimate and that they will be satisfied with the increase in basic rates and the raising of the ceiling on permissible incomes which will be provided in the amendments to be submitted by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe).
I am pleased to note that some amendments will be made to the Blind Persons Act. I cannot think of a greater handicap any person can have than blindness. These blind persons bear their burdens cheerfully and admirably. During the past three months I have had occasion to visit the blind persons of our community. Many of them said to me that they find it most difficult to provide a normal existence for themselves. I should like to congratulate the Canadian National Institute for the Blind on providing some

education for leaders whose duty it is to supervise the activities of blind people and to plan entertainment and recreational facilities for them. Training courses in arts and crafts enable the blind to supplement their small pensions. We provide for them the opportunity to conduct curio booths and newsstands in our public buddings, railway depots and hospital foyers.
If these people have the industry, initiative and courage to develop their talents, and if they have the perseverance and ability to earn small incomes, I believe they should be given some special preferment in the matter of their earnings. Although it may not be provided in the present amendments, I look forward to the day when blind persons may be able to accept pensions without the imposition of a means test at all.
I was happy to note that the administration intends to embark on a satisfactory policy of public works. The people of St. Catharines, whom I have the honour to represent, are gratified that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) has seen fit to provide a federal public building in that city. This accommodation is greatly needed in a community that has shown unusual expansion in the past decade. There is a great need for proper accommodation for federal offices in our community.
We feel that we have another public works project in our area that requires immediate attention. I refer to the clean-up of the old Welland canal. Three canals have been built across the face of the Niagara peninsula by federal governments during the past century. These canals were built to provide a more expeditious route for shipping to avoid the natural barrier at Niagara Falls. The unused Welland canal, which passes through Thorold, Merritton, St. Catharines and Port Dalhousie, has become an unsightly, pestilential cesspool. The municipal governments in the area have come to an agreement as to the method that should be followed in cleaning up this unsightly mess. They have decided to remove the locks, fill in the banks and narrow the channel.
I say the municipalities have come to an agreement. They have agreed on the method of construction. They have not agreed as to the proportion of cost, and it is hoped that the Department of Transport will be generous to these municipalities in its contribution toward the cost of construction. In addition to improving the general contour of the area, the project will provide useful employment for residents of the adjoining municipalities.

I should like also to bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) a difficulty which has arisen near the Welland canal. The present Welland ship canal is crossed by the Queen Elizabeth way in the township of Grantham at Homer. By reason of the fact that the bridge must be raised and lowered many times during the shipping season, frequent interruptions have caused great delay and confusion in the traffic which travels along the Queen Elizabeth way. I hope that engineers of the Department of Transport and the Ontario department of highways may devise some method which will relieve this confusion and avoid the bottleneck that now exists. It is a matter that requires the co-operation of the two levels of government. An early meeting, I hope, will be held when some of the residents of our area will discuss the matter in a more elaborate way with the Minister of Transport.
This is not a problem which concerns only the residents of my constituency, although they are directly affected. It is of indirect concern to the travelling public of many provinces of Canada, and many of our guests who come from several of the states of the union to the south.
During the past six weeks Canadian ministers of the crown have been engaged in endeavouring to get the United States of America and the United Kingdom to agree to certain provisions for the overhaul of the general agreement on tariffs and trade. Great efforts have been made by the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who has attended negotiations in London' Washington and Geneva. While the efforts he has made have not met with the success we would like, I am convinced that the situation will clarify itself. Present reports coming from Washington indicate that the President and congress may be more amenable in the future. It was encouraging to hear the minister say that further efforts would be made to see if this agreement could be carried out. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has been quoted as saying that "the collapse of GATT would be the worst possible thing that could happen; it would be a catastrophe to the free world." It is our hope that an agreement may still be reached which will be mutually advantageous to ourselves and to all other member nations.
I should not allow this opportunity to pass without saying something about the proposal to amend the rules of this house. We heard the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) say yesterday that this subject would be handed to a special committee for discussion during this session. I am sure that the amendment of our rules would do much to expedite the

The Prime Minister endeavoured to give us some idea of his thinking in the matter when he arranged that the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne would speak on the same day as the address itself was delivered. This would indicate to me a desire on his part that we should make better use of the time at our disposal here.
It is my opinion that the speeches of private members should be limited to 20 minutes. I believe the proposal would be to limit speeches to 30 minutes.

I believe I have spoken for about 18 minutes. The Prime Minister and members of the cabinet, the leader and certain designated members of the opposition, the leader of the C.C.F. group and the leader of the Social Credit group might be given 40 minutes. It seems to me that the average member in this house could very well clarify his thoughts and present them within a period of 20 minutes. I believe also that a limited time could be allocated for the speech from the throne and the budget debate. This would not deprive any member of the opportunity to speak, but it would improve the quality of debate and shorten the length of the session.
I have addressed groups throughout my constituency on this subject in order to gain some idea of how our constituents feel about the matter. I have talked with others in private conversation. The Canadian people do not wish to lose respect for parliament, but they do feel we should conduct the affairs

of the nation in a businesslike and efficient manner and with reasonable dispatch. They ask us to give them an honest and conscientious administration of affairs. We can do this without long, laboured addresses in this chamber. When these amendments are presented, I feel it will be a step in the right direction, and the measure should receive support from all parts of the house.
I have been reminded that I have spoken for some time. I think I have now completed 20 minutes, so I thank you, gentlemen.
